families.s: HSE engineering solutions for repeated food-sector handling tasks
families.t: mechanisation, lifting aids, task redesign, worker involvement, trialling, training, fatigue and monitoring
f: HSE food-sector case studies emphasise practical and cost-effective controls.
Mechanical transfer equipment can remove repetitive lifting from high-frequency tasks.
Cradles, conveyors and lifting aids can improve positioning and reduce awkward handling.
Task redesign can reduce both manual-handling risk and worker-animal interaction.
Workers should be involved in planning, equipment trials and training material.
Control effectiveness should be checked after installation.
Bulk storage and vacuum lifting can eliminate or reduce unit-load handling.
Where full mechanisation is not practicable, lift-assist devices and work-height adjustment should be considered.

families.s: HSE control of cold work and entrapment in chilled and frozen food production
families.t: workroom temperature, local chilling, thermal clothing, warming breaks, blast freezers, health, escape and alarms
f: Food hygiene temperatures and worker air-temperature duties address different things and can be met together.
Open workrooms should normally maintain a reasonable temperature.
Localised refrigeration can protect food without chilling the whole workroom.
Warm workstations, thermal clothing, task rotation and warming breaks can reduce cold stress.
Around 0°C, suitable clothing and normal breaks may be sufficient depending on the assessment.
At blast-freezer temperatures around -30°C, warming breaks are necessary because PPE alone is insufficient.
Risk assessment should consider respiratory, circulatory and noise-related health conditions.
Walk-in chillers and freezers need internal escape, visible release devices and, where appropriate, trapped-person alarms.

families.s: HSE organisational learning from food and drink control case studies
families.t: shared learning, practical controls, leadership, worker involvement, verification, cost effectiveness, rehabilitation, review
f: HSE publishes food and drink case studies so organisations can share practical controls.
The examples cover manual handling, slips, falls, transport, machinery, asthma, noise and dermatitis.
Case studies describe the original problem, selected solution and measured outcome.
Engineering changes are preferred where they remove exposure or dangerous interaction.
Leadership is needed to plan, purchase and implement new controls.
Worker participation improves usability and acceptance.
Training and documentation should be updated when controls change.
The Food and Drink Manufacture Forum supports joint prioritisation and sector learning.

families.s: HSE protection of migrant workers in food processing and other high-risk sectors
families.t: competence, induction, language, understandable information, supervision, emergencies, buddy systems and rights
f: Health and safety law protects migrant workers in the same way as other workers.
New workers may face unfamiliar work, risks, rights and safety systems.
Employers should assess language, literacy, numeracy, health, experience and relevant qualifications before work starts.
Induction should use plain language and explain hazards, precautions and safety equipment.
Employers should check that workers understand training and emergency procedures.
Supervision should be adequate and communication with supervisors effective.
Information need not be in English if risks, controls and emergencies are clearly communicated.
Interpreters, buddy systems, visual material, signs and trained supervisors can reduce language barriers.

families.s: HSE risk assessment and consultation for farms and growers
families.t: hazards, workers, contractors, public, vulnerable people, priorities, written findings, review and consultation
f: Agricultural employers must protect employees and others affected by work so far as reasonably practicable.
Risk assessment is a careful examination of what could harm people and whether more precautions are needed.
Hazards should be identified by observation, experience, worker input and manufacturer information.
Assessments should consider casual workers, trainees, contractors, neighbours and the public.
Vulnerable people such as young, new or expectant workers need particular consideration.
The most serious risks should be addressed first.
Significant findings must be recorded when five or more people are employed.
Controls should be checked and assessments reviewed after change and periodically.
